issues.legal_issue: An appellant cannot renew a grievance about a prosecution withdrawal after an order affirming that withdrawal has become final because it was not challenged.
material_facts: A prosecution against the appellant’s opposing party was withdrawn with the court’s consent on an application by the Public Prosecutor.
The appellant challenged the withdrawal in a criminal revision, which the High Court dismissed in 1991.
The appellant did not challenge that revision judgment, which had become final before the later proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The appellant had no surviving grievance about the withdrawn prosecution and could not rely on it to challenge the later orders.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 321 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the discretion to seek withdrawal belongs to the Public Prosecutor, who must not surrender it to another person; withdrawal may rest on relevant considerations beyond lack of evidence, and the court must scrutinize the application for extraneous considerations. In this case, the earlier revision judgment affirming the withdrawal became final and was not challenged; no earlier cases are cited.

predicates.appeal_against_later_writ_orders: The appellant appealed orders made in later writ and recall proceedings.
predicates.earlier_revision_upholding_withdrawal_fi: A prior revision judgment upheld the withdrawal of a prosecution and became final.
predicates.appellant_did_not_challenge_revision: The appellant did not challenge the prior revision judgment.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns later writ orders, an unchallenged final revision judgment upholding a prosecution withdrawal means the appellant has no surviving grievance about that withdrawal.

issues.legal_issue: A direction to register a case and proceed according to law is sustainable where an inquiry and medical evidence support a complaint of police inaction concerning injuries.
material_facts: A complainant alleged that he and his sons had been attacked and injured, and that the police had not registered his complaint or taken action.
A court-directed inquiry by a senior police officer produced a report, and medical examination confirmed injuries to the complainant.
The High Court directed the competent police authority to register a case and take action according to law, and declined to recall that direction.
The appellant objected in part on the basis of delay and his prior dispute and prosecution involving the complainant.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no infirmity in the High Court’s directions or its refusal to recall them and dismissed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: On the facts, the confirmed injuries and the inquiry report supported the High Court’s direction for police action. The Court found no infirmity in the orders and no ground for interference; it cited no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this conclusion.

rule.if: appeal_against_writ_and_recall_orders and complaint_of_police_inaction and injuries_medically_confirmed and court_directed_inquiry_supported_complaint

predicates.appeal_against_writ_and_recall_orders: The appellant challenged orders made in writ proceedings and in an application seeking recall of those orders.
predicates.complaint_of_police_inaction: A complainant said the police had not registered a complaint or taken action concerning an alleged incident.
predicates.injuries_medically_confirmed: Medical examination confirmed injuries to the complainant.
predicates.court_directed_inquiry_supported_complai: An inquiry conducted at the court’s direction produced a report supporting the complaint.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges writ and recall orders, and a complaint of police inaction is supported by confirmed injuries and a court-directed inquiry, the direction for registration and investigation stands.
